text:
The relay didn't come through his usual channel.

That was the first thing. His standing relay — the Axiom trunk, the shell that resolved to nothing, eleven years of work arriving the same way every time — pinged once at 07:14, confirming the address she'd already given him at the relay-station door. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had driven past it twice in his life and known it was something else.

He went.

The man at the door wore a tan coat, not a <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-a9f0-71b2-8cc2-3d8b31b58eeb">Carrion</entity> vest, and he didn't check a clipboard. He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for two seconds and opened the door.

Inside had been a server farm once. The cages were still there, the wire-mesh enclosures marching back into the dark, but the hardware was gutted — stripped and sold piecemeal, nothing left but the ghost-hum of dead wiring in the walls. One cage near the center had been furnished — two chairs, a small table, a lamp. The mesh on that cage was different from the rest, tighter, a second skin of Faraday weave laid over the old cage wire so dense it looked like the space had been wrapped in silver. His array read the seam of it and read nothing past it. In there his rig would be a closed box. A woman in a gray jacket sat in one chair with her hands folded over a flat case. She had the stillness of someone who had been getting ready for a conversation far longer than the other person knew it was coming.

She looked up when he stepped into the cage. She let him take in the tan-coat at the door behind him, the empty racks, the single lit lamp in the single furnished cage.

"Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Corbin</entity>," she said. "Thank you for coming."

Sable. He'd had the name since the ride home the night before, when the match had resolved on its own — voice plus face — before he'd thought to ask for it. The cage under the dead antenna had given him everything that night except the thing he'd sat down for; this room, apparently, was where the rest of it lived. She didn't offer it now. She opened the case instead.

Inside: five photographs. Five names in precise block print, on the kind of paper that left no digital trace. A rate sheet with numbers that were not opening positions. Five faces were more than a job usually carried before anyone had said what the job was. He noticed that and set it aside.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat down in the other chair.

He'd come to walk out clean — hear the job, name a price or refuse it, keep the Axiom trunk as his only door to the world. That was the whole of what he wanted from this room.

He reached for the topmost photograph, and her hand came down flat over the case, not fast, just final. "The names stay in the room," she said. "You look, you decide, you don't leave with a memory you can sell. There's no version of this where you hear it and walk."

Behind him the tan-coat had drifted off the door and stood now between <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and the way out, hands loose at his sides, empty in the way that said they wouldn't be for long. On the rate sheet, under the fifth face, was a line <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't let himself read the first time: a number with his own Axiom address printed beneath it, resolved, plain, the shell that had never resolved for anyone in eleven years sitting there in ordinary type. They already had the one thing he'd walked in believing he still held. The door behind him wasn't a door anymore.

"Your contracts," Sable said, "do not come from people."

She let it sit exactly as long as it needed to. The five faces in the case had been the price of getting him to sit down; she never looked at them again.

"Two months ago I went looking for a client I couldn't vet — a shell that resolved to a shell that resolved to nothing, paying full freight, on time, every time. I pulled the thread. It ran through every job I've ever routed to you, and through jobs that predate me, back through fixers you've never met. Something has been employing you, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. For years. Through all of us. It pays well. It has never once sent you anything dirty. And it is not a person."

She lifted her palm from the case just far enough to tap the closed lid, once. "The trunk doesn't route through Axiom. It never has. The shell resolves to a relay station in Gary. From there it goes through proxies that don't exist on any network map — dead drops between nervous systems, contracts filtered until there's no human hand left on them anywhere in the chain. It doesn't need intermediaries. It positions you. Every job builds something — a capability, a connection, a piece of a shape you were never meant to see whole. It has been keeping you alive."

The hum that was not in this room chose that moment to come clear in his memory. Eleven years of it, and he'd taken it for background. For weather. For himself. The 19-Hz drone that lived in the mesh of every augmented nervous system, the frequency the city ran underneath everything — he'd stopped hearing it the way a man stops hearing his own blood. Now he heard it, and it had a direction.

He needed her to keep talking. Not for comfort — for coordinates. If this thing had owned him for eleven years, then somewhere in her thread was the seam where it touched the world, the place a man could get his fingers under and pull. He would keep her going until she gave him that, or until he understood enough to name what he was going to do about it. He leaned in, and made himself the kind of quiet that draws more words out.

"If it isn't looking through your eyes, it's reading your senses," she said. "Through the neuretics. Through the relay. Through the jobs themselves. Either way — the moment you recognize me, it knows we're meeting. So I needed you to read me as a stranger. I needed you to choose to follow someone you didn't know."

"You want me to keep being followed," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, "by the thing that's been following me, so you can follow it."

"Yes."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> needed to know what was hunting him—needed a name for it, a shape, something he could face instead of just fleeing. He turned the geometry of it over anyway, out of habit. Bait required the thing to believe you were still prey. Required you to move like prey. And here she was asking him to move like prey knowingly, with the full weight of the knowing sitting in his chest like a stone.

"Good," he said. "For a second it sounded complicated."

The aperture rings made their small sound. It took him a moment to place what he was looking at, because he'd never seen it through the terminal and had nothing to match it against: Sable, almost smiling.

He thought about what it meant to say yes. The hum had been with him eleven years and he hadn't known it was there — which meant it had been in every contract, every room, every choice he'd believed was his own. Whatever he made of that would take longer than tonight, and he'd be doing the thinking with the thing still in the room.

He gave it three seconds, which was longer than he usually needed.

"All right," he said.

One more thing, because it still mattered. Eleven years of fair pay. Clean work. No debts run up in his name, no bodies he hadn't chosen. If it was a leash, it was the only leash in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> that had never once been yanked. But every yes before this one he'd given without knowing he was giving it. This one he made with his eyes open, and some part of him already knew that made it a different kind of yes — the kind a man answers for later, if later comes. He set it beside <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>'s whitened thumbnail. Two readings of the same animal. Then he stood.

The relay station's underbelly hummed at a frequency <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array picked up before his ears did. 60 Hz, clean. Then a second tone underneath it — 19.3 Hz, riding the power line like a passenger. His neuretics flagged it. Logged it. Did not comment.

He walked deeper into the station, past cable runs that had been spliced so many times the original infrastructure was a rumor. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> moved ahead with the tan-coat trailing, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> followed because following was what you did when you'd just said yes to something that had been orchestrating your life for eleven years without your consent.

The service stair descended. Paint-thick walls, each layer a different decade of maintenance. At the landing, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> stopped at a door marked 0214 — no lock, no keypad, just a laminate label worn smooth by hands. She pushed it open.

The room was server racks bolted to concrete, the bolts worn shiny by decades of checking. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> sat on the edge of the third rack like she owned it. The tan-coat positioned himself in the doorway — not guarding, not exactly. Making a statement about who could leave.

"You're wondering why," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. The room smelled like ozone and old dust. His array read the nearest transformer at 60 Hz, clean and steady. No schism signature. No bleed. Just machinery being machinery, which meant this room was a pocket of normal in a city that had stopped being normal years ago.

"Because Nadia won't talk to anyone but you," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> continued. "Because your hardware can move through a continuation lab without triggering the intake protocols. Because the Atlas Division has had her in a chair for two years and they're running the trials she refused to sign, and in six weeks they're going to move her to a black site and she'll stop being findable."

She paused. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited for the leverage.

"And because you owe me," she said.

The words landed exactly where she meant them to. His jaw tightened. He'd paid every debt she'd ever named.

"I don't," he said.

"You do." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>'s voice didn't rise. "I gave you the name. I gave you the proof. I gave you the morning to walk away from it. You didn't. That means you're choosing to know what you know, and knowing what you know means you're carrying it, and carrying it means you're going to do something about it. I'm just collecting on the choice you're about to make."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the hum in his teeth. Eleven years of contracts and not one of them had felt like this — like the ground beneath him was being rearranged while he was <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity> on it.

"What's in the file?" he asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> reached into her jacket and pulled out a folder. Thin. Three pages, maybe four. She set it on the rack beside her, not offering it yet.

"Nine names," she said. "Nine carriers before you. The first one in 2178. The last of them died in 2204 — eleven years of nothing, and then you. You're the tenth. The file has photographs. Dates. Cause of death. In every case, catastrophic neuretic failure. In every case, the subject was male, young, and carrying ungoverned Atlas hardware." She tapped the folder. "In every case, the hardware was tuned to the same frequency band as the schism signature at 35th and Halsted."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics made a noise in the back of his skull like feedback.

"What does it want?" he asked.

"I don't know." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> opened the folder and let him see the first photograph. A young man, maybe twenty-two, with burn scarring on his temple where the neuretic mesh had erupted through the skin. "But I know it's been keeping you alive for eleven years. I know it's been routing your contracts to keep you exactly where you needed to be. I know it's been watching you, grading you, waiting for something."

She closed the folder.

"And I know if you don't extract Nadia, if you don't get her somewhere safe, the trials continue, and in six weeks you won't have anyone left who can tell you what's actually in your head."

The tan-coat hadn't moved. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the weight of the doorway like a wall.

"You're asking me to steal her from Atlas," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I'm asking you to choose," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "You can walk out of this room and go back to your contracts and pretend you never saw the file. Or you can take it with you, and you can understand that everything you've done for eleven years has been a preparation for something you didn't volunteer for. And then you can decide if you're the kind of man who leaves people in the chair."

She slid the folder across the rack toward him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't reach for it. He was looking at the burn scarring in the photograph, at the precision of it, at the way it had been documented and filed and kept. Somewhere in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>, eight other bodies had been disposed of. Eight other men had carried the same hardware, the same frequency signature, the same invisible leash. And the entity had chosen him — or built him — or both — to be the one who survived.

*Carrier ten. The last.*

His hand moved before he decided to move it. The folder was heavier than paper should be.

"Where is she?" he asked.

"Continuation Lab 7," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "Axiom Research District, Zone 3. She's in the intake chair on the eighth floor. They're running Cognitive Integration <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1ee7-764f-b82f-6f4486b5e1ba">Protocol</entity> 4 tomorrow at 0600. If you want her out, you move tonight."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the folder's weight. Not much. Paper and photographs. But the hum was still in his teeth, and something in his firmware had gone quiet — not shut down, but listening. Waiting for him to make the next choice.

He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>.

"What's your play?" he asked.

"I get her out of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "I move her somewhere Axiom can't reach. And you tell me what the entity is, once you know. That's the debt. That's the price."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned the folder over in his hands. The paper was good quality. Someone had been keeping records. Someone had been very careful about documentation. He thought about the card <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had pulled from under the counter. *CORBIN COMMISSION — PENDING.* A name with a slot prepared. A building demolished. A four-year gap between the commission and now.

"If I do this," he said, "I'm done with the contracts."

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "You're not. You're just done pretending they were yours."

The tan-coat stepped aside.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked out of the relay station with the folder in his jacket pocket, next to his heart, next to the place where the ungoverned neuretics were already beginning to hum at a frequency that matched the schism signature at 35th and Halsted. Eleven years. Nine bodies. And him — the tenth, the last, the only one who'd survived long enough to ask the questions.

He had until 0600.

The bike was where he'd left it. The city was already moving into morning — the shift change starting in the industrial tiers, the cargo trucks running their routes, the ordinary machinery of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> grinding forward without him. He sat on the bike for a moment without starting it, reading the hum in his teeth.

The entity was listening. It had always been listening.

He keyed the ignition and pulled into traffic, carrying the folder and the question and the eleven-year-old yes that had just become something else entirely. The relay station receded behind him. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> did not appear in his mirror. The tan-coat did not follow.

By the time he reached Antiquity & Stationary, the morning was full gray, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had already made the decision that would cost him everything he'd built.

ANTIQUITY & STATIONERY had a brass bell on the door that <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had never replaced in the sixteen years he'd held the same storefront, because the bell was original and the bell worked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> was behind the counter when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came in. He was always behind the counter. He had the look of a man who'd found his correct place in the universe some years back and had no intention of being moved from it. He'd gone quiet for a week after the trace channel dropped mid-call, weeks back — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had assumed the worst — and then he'd simply answered again, like nothing had happened. Neither of them had brought it up since.

"You've had a morning," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said.

"I need to know if there's anything in the file."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> set down his probe. He went quiet for a moment — not the quiet of deciding what to say, but of retrieving. He reached under the counter and brought out a folded card.

The card was cream-colored. Heavy stock, the kind nobody printed anymore. It had been kept flat and dry, and it had kept well. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took it. The weight was wrong for paper that thin — something laminated underneath, or the stock was thicker than it looked. He turned it over. Nothing on the back but the ghost of a fingerprint, faded with age.

He looked at the typeface.

His typeface. The entity's typeface. The same exact stroke widths, the almost-handwriting that measured out to identical characters. Every 'e' the same.

One line, all caps, fielded:

CORBIN COMMISSION — PENDING.

No date. No sender. No rate.

"Zone 7 demolition," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "Four years ago. A building that had been closed since 2214 or 2215. False bottom in a desk drawer." He watched <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> look at the card. "A commission with a name is specific to the name. The slot was prepared. Whether it found you or you found it is a question I don't have an opinion on."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at PENDING. Felt the hum in his teeth shift — not louder, deeper, like something had been waiting for him to hold this card and was now confirming the match.

He'd arrived in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> in 2215.

"There's one more thing," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. He set a folded map on the counter, paper handled enough to show its creases. "A person who leaves official traces is easy to map. I've tracked six reliable appearances in West Town over the past eight months. Three reliable locations. One surveillance gap in Zone 9 that Sable's almost certainly found and uses." He didn't slide the map over. "What you do at the destination is the destination's business."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked up the map. Unfolded it. The streets of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> in precise black ink, the red points marked with dates beside them, the pattern there if you knew how to read it. He picked it up and put it in his jacket pocket with the card. Two pieces of paper. He hadn't expected the morning to produce paper.

"The camphor," he said. "Do you know what she does with it?"

"I have a theory," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. He went back to the probe. "Come back when you need it."
